doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Craft versus soul in the L.A. studio scene
summary: Reacting to two quotes, Mays agrees with the positive one and says Shank and Manne kept playing jazz.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Before we leave Los Angeles so to speak, I wanted to read two quotes from gentlemen who were incredibly successful in that scene but they had different feelings about it. And they’ll remain anonymous but I know that you would know of them. The first fellow said, “L.A. is an incredible place for craft. You really learn to play your instrument, to play in tune, to show up on time, all of the essentials for a craft are there but your soul, your spirit, is not usually nurtured.” The second fellow said, “Our job was to go in there and play with one another, which we took great joy in doing and whatever the music is man, we’ll just nail it. So that was soul-gratifying, just to do that, regardless of the artist.

Well I certainly agree with the second quote and the first one sounds pretty pessimistic and I knew a lot of great studio players who could also play jazz – I won’t mention names – but they would not go out and play jazz. And then there were people like Bud Shank and Shelly Manne who were great studio musicians and also loved jazz and kept their jazz careers going at the same time, as I did. I really enjoyed studio work 90 percent of the time. I enjoyed the craft, I enjoyed playing various instruments: harpsichord, organ, synthesizers, electric piano, calliope.
